what purpose do towns like that serve? i mean, is it a farm town or something?

Generally, when a town was founded, there was a reason for it being there; in the case of Ricketts, it was a stop on a railroad line that no longer exists (I think it was torn up for it's steel for the war effort). A railroad stop was an important feature when many tons of crops had to be carried by wagon to the railway station, because it meant that much less time and effort hauling the harvest. This has all been made obsolete by the 18-wheel truck. In other cases, where a town is geographically isolated, the population remains because the land is cheap due to it's isolation, it has some feature like good soil or a microclimate for growing a lucrative crop, or basically they're just too stubborn or set in their ways to leave.

In the case of really old towns, it seems that many of our forefathers were not as bright as we give them credit for (at least this seems to be the trend that I have seen when doing genealogy research). A small group of people would travel weeks or months getting across the prairie, and would camp for a night at a rather pleasant place and end up staying; in essence, they would get tired of living out of a wooden and cloth wagon, say, "screw it", take a vote, and say, "let's just settle here, this looks good". Others would come along, see the nice place they set up and would stay as well. This is how many settlements would grow up along the wagon trails during the westward expansion. The land would be just enough to support a moderate amount of people, and would not have the resources (like navigable rivers or level land for future railroads) to support a city. If a better piece of land was available 30 or 50 miles away, other people would build a city there, and the first settlers would end up living in what would become a backwater, or as can be seen all through the western us, they would end up as ghost towns. Early settlers that became landowners of vast tracts and had cities and counties named after them were the ones that bought maps, did surveys, and did their research before deciding where to settle; George Washington was a surveyor, and look how much he accomplished.
